section_summary: This section concludes a Civil Affairs Guide recommending that the occupation authorities legalize democratic trade unions, abolish coercive labor institutions and laws, regulate collective bargaining and strikes, and establish machinery for settling industrial disputes. Its appendices list prewar unions and officials, summarize union membership and labor-dispute statistics, and reproduce selected repressive legislation. The section then documents Japan’s December 1945 Trade Union Law, early postwar union growth, State Department comments on the law, and difficulties arranging labor-union advisers for a commission to Japan.

subfiles.title: Civil Affairs Guide: Trade Unions and Labor Relations in Japan, concluding recommendations and appendices
subfiles.about: Recommends an occupation policy for democratizing Japanese labor relations and supplies supporting data and texts of repressive laws.
subfiles.summary: The guide calls for freedom of labor organization and speech, repeal of laws used against unions, release of labor prisoners, and dissolution of Sampo and associated organizations. It proposes rules for collective bargaining, strikes, mediation, arbitration, minimum standards, and a Military Government labor section, while recommending the abolition of repressive agencies and exclusion of compromised personnel. Appendices list major prewar unions and their leaders, present statistics on membership and disputes, and reproduce portions of the Peace Preservation Law, protective-surveillance legislation, National Mobilization Law, Public Peace Police Law, and Police Crimes Punishment Law.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 146: Transmitting Copy of Trade Union Law
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Trade Union Law passed by the 89th Imperial Diet and promulgated on December 21, 1945.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 146 forwards copies of Japan's newly enacted Trade Union Law, with the original and a hectograph copy to the Department.

subfiles.title: Trade Union Law, Law No. 51
subfiles.from: Emperor Hirohito and the Japanese Cabinet
subfiles.about: Promulgates Japan's postwar legal framework for trade unions, collective agreements, labor-relations committees, and penalties.
subfiles.summary: The law guarantees workers' organization and collective bargaining while defining qualifying unions, protected activities, registration rules, legal personality, and grounds for dissolution. It prohibits anti-union discrimination, regulates trade agreements, and permits their extension to other workers in a workplace or locality. It also creates national, prefectural, and special Labor Relations Committees for investigation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, and the recommendation of labor standards, with penalties for specified violations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 184: Formation of Labor Unions in Japan
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Transmits Ministry of Welfare statistics on Japanese labor-union organization and membership as of December 12, 1945.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson forwards a Mainichi tabulation of new unions credited to the Welfare Ministry; membership of about 120,000 probably already surpassed.

subfiles.title: Labor Unions: Ministry of Welfare Statistical Tabulation
subfiles.from: Ministry of Welfare, as reported by the Mainichi
subfiles.to: Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Tabulates unions, members, labor troubles, and strikes by industry and identifies large unions then being organized.
subfiles.summary: Ministry of Welfare table: 45 unions with 74,434 members through December 12 plus twenty unreported; Yahata and Mitsui Omuta unions would bring the total to about 120,000-130,000.

subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Ernest Gross concerning comments on Japan's Trade Union Law
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.to: Lieutenant Colonel Ernest Gross, Civil Affairs Division, War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards Philip Sullivan's comments on Japan's Trade Union Law and proposes sending their substance to SCAP as State Department comments.
subfiles.summary: Martin sends Gross Philip Sullivan's comments on Japanese Law 51, recommending most go to SCAP with a qualification that timing is for the Supreme Commander, and asks Gross's views.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: CIO Representative on Labor Commission to Japan
subfiles.to: Department of State files; copies to Thorp, Wilcox, and Mulliken
subfiles.about: Records discussions about transportation delays and possible replacement of the CIO adviser assigned to the Labor Commission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mike Ross says CIO adviser McCreedy might decline the Labor Commission mission for lack of air transport; Sullivan urges a replacement and stresses the mission's importance.
